02 · Quantification

Detection probability curve, protein roll-up, detection filter, normalisation

Half of a DIA matrix is empty, and not at random: faint precursors go missing more often than bright ones. dpc() fits that as a curve, and dpcQuant() uses it to give every protein a value in every sample without imputing anything. This stage is the limpa vignette’s own sequence, unaltered.

The missingness relationship

plotAveVsMis(y)

A downward trend means detection depends on intensity and the DPC has something to fit. A flat cloud would mean missingness is closer to random, where limpa still works but gains less over simpler methods.

The curve

dpcest <- dpc(y$E)
plotDPC(dpcest)
dpc_parameters <- tibble(
  intercept = dpcest$dpc[1],
  slope = dpcest$dpc[2]
)
round(dpc_parameters, 3)
intercept slope
-8.958 0.488

dpc() defaults to model = "cn" and its help says it then returns dpcCN(), the complete-normal estimator the limpa FAQ recommends for noisy data. Its subset = 2000 default fits on a systematic sample stratified by missingness and mean intensity rather than all 47,133 rows. limpa documents robust as “Only used if `model=‘on’”, so it does nothing here and the subsample supplies the robustness.

The fit comes out at 0.488, below the 0.7-to-0.9 band the FAQ calls typical for DIA-NN searched with match-between-runs, though inside the 0.1-to-1.0 range it calls usable. The vignette notes the slope comes out low when peptides vary a lot, which is what a within-subject design with heavy missingness looks like.

Quantification therefore uses a preset 0.7, which is the rule limpa’s FAQ gives for this exact situation: “If dpcCN() doesn’t give a value in that range, it would be reasonable to run dpcQuant() with a preset value dpc.slope=0.7.” The fitted value is carried into a sensitivity run at the end. The choice follows the documented rule, not any downstream count.

One caveat belongs on the record. The FAQ says a slope set too low makes the analysis more conservative. On this data the reverse held when it was last measured: the lower fitted slope gave smaller standard errors and more hits than the preset. The preset is still both the documented setting and the cautious one here, but the direction is not what the documentation predicts.

Note

The visual fit is not the diagnostic. plotDPC() draws a curve in unobserved intensity against proportions computed on observed intensity, so some discrepancy is structural. Judge the slope.

Roll-up

dpcQuant() fits an additive precursor-plus-sample model per protein, maximising a posterior that scores observed values by squared residual and missing values by their DPC probability. The returned $other$standard.error is why this project uses limpa: dpcDE() reads it as a precision weight, so a protein reconstructed largely from missing precursors gets a value and a wide one. Handing $E to lmFit() discards that and treats every protein as equally reliable.

The call itself lives in a_script/dpc_quant.R, not here, because it costs about 100 minutes. This notebook only loads what that script wrote, so rendering is always cheap and can never start a long run by accident. Rerun the script by hand when the precursor matrix changes.

if (!file.exists(primary_file)) {
  stop("No dpcQuant checkpoint. Run:\n",
    "  Rscript 01_Preprocess/02_Quantification/a_script/dpc_quant.R")
}
proteins <- readRDS(primary_file)$object

3,451 protein groups from 47,133 precursors. The matrix has no missing values; what varies is how certain each value is.

Detection filter

filterByDetection()’s help fixes the order: it runs after dpcQuant() and before DE, and it returns a logical vector rather than an object. For a small experiment the help suggests setting n.samples to the smallest group size. Here that is BFR_T2 with 32 samples, one short because nobody acquired S06’s left leg at T2.

The function does not read group. It counts detections across all samples and keeps a protein when that count clears the threshold, so the smallest group size sets a cohort-wide bar rather than guaranteeing detection within any one group.

group_sizes <- table(proteins$targets$group)
keep <- filterByDetection(proteins, n.samples = min(group_sizes))
proteins <- proteins[keep, ]

group_sizes

 BFR_T1  BFR_T2 HLRT_T1 HLRT_T2 
     33      32      33      33 
c(before = length(keep), kept = sum(keep), dropped = sum(!keep))
 before    kept dropped 
   3451    3042     409

The proteins this drops are not borderline. Measured on an earlier run, they carried a mean standard error of 1.56 against 0.66 for those kept, and 0.15 detected precursors per sample against 7.48, so the typical sample measured nothing at all for them. Relaxing the threshold to limpa’s default of 3 recovered 371 of them, of which exactly one reached BH < 0.05 in any contrast, while the extra tests cost 14 and 29 proteins on the two training contrasts.

Normalisation

limpa places normalisation after dpcQuant() and before dpcDE() and performs none itself, because DIA-NN has usually normalised the precursors already. What matters is which kind is needed, and two numbers separate the cases.

The spread in per-sample medians is what a single per-sample shift would fix. The MA curve width is what only cyclic loess fixes: comparing a sample against the average of all samples gives a difference per protein, and fitting that against abundance gives a curve. A flat curve means the sample disagrees by a constant. A curve that travels means the disagreement depends on abundance. Both numbers are reported before and after so the correction can be judged rather than assumed.

ma_width <- function(E) {
  a <- rowMeans(E)
  apply(E, 2, \(x) diff(range(lowess(a, x - a, f = 0.5)$y)))
}
spread <- function(E) diff(range(apply(E, 2, median)))

before <- c(ma_width = median(ma_width(proteins$E)), median_spread = spread(proteins$E))
proteins$E <- normalizeBetweenArrays(proteins$E, method = "cyclicloess")
after <- c(ma_width = median(ma_width(proteins$E)), median_spread = spread(proteins$E))

round(rbind(before, after), 3)
       ma_width median_spread
before    0.448         1.175
after     0.161         0.430

The curvature is unrelated to treatment or timepoint, so cyclic loess is not absorbing the effect being tested. proteins.rds is written after this, so it is the matrix the model is fitted to.

WarningAn approximation, stated plainly

Cyclic loess remaps $E non-linearly while $other$standard.error is left untouched. After normalisation the stored errors describe the unnormalised scale and dpcDE() reads them as though they described the new one. Smyth recommends quantile and cyclic loess for this data regardless, and the mapping is close enough to linear that the discrepancy is small, but it is an approximation rather than an exact correspondence.

What survives

protein_quality <- tibble(
  protein = rownames(proteins),
  gene = proteins$genes$Genes,
  n_precursors = proteins$genes$NPrec,
  prop_observed = proteins$genes$PropObs,
  mean_log2 = rowMeans(proteins$E),
  mean_standard_error = rowMeans(proteins$other$standard.error),
  mean_n_observations = rowMeans(proteins$other$n.observations)
)
summary(protein_quality[c("mean_log2", "mean_standard_error", "prop_observed")])
   mean_log2     mean_standard_error prop_observed    
 Min.   :12.98   Min.   :0.03107     Min.   :0.03716  
 1st Qu.:16.07   1st Qu.:0.38500     1st Qu.:0.30245  
 Median :17.10   Median :0.58428     Median :0.42324  
 Mean   :17.53   Mean   :0.65862     Mean   :0.43278  
 3rd Qu.:18.63   3rd Qu.:0.91420     3rd Qu.:0.54962  
 Max.   :26.79   Max.   :1.50131     Max.   :0.97710

NPrec is what the installed version writes; the help page calls it NPeptides. A protein with a high mean standard error and few observations is one whose estimate leans on the DPC rather than on data.

Points are coloured by participant, and the variance each factor explains in the leading dimension is printed below the plot. Thirty-two of the 33 participants contribute all four cells, so between-participant variation dominates and the participant term in the design is what removes it. A sample sitting far from its own participant is worth investigating; an absence of group structure is not.

mds <- plotMDSUsingSEs(proteins,
  pch = 16,
  col = as.integer(factor(proteins$targets$participant))
)
r2 <- function(f) summary(lm(mds$x ~ factor(f)))$r.squared
round(c(
  participant = r2(proteins$targets$participant),
  group = r2(proteins$targets$group)
), 3)
participant       group 
      0.515       0.027

Slope sensitivity

Quantification is repeated at the fitted slope and compared against the primary run, with the same detection filter and normalisation applied so the slope is the only difference. dpcDE() reads the standard errors as precision weights, so whichever run carries the larger mean is the more conservative setting.

The median absolute difference in protein abundance follows the table. It measures how far values move, not whether that movement survives a contrast: every comparison here is within one participant, so a shift common to a participant’s samples cancels in the subtraction.

sensitivity <- readRDS(sensitivity_file)$object
sensitivity <- sensitivity[filterByDetection(sensitivity, n.samples = min(group_sizes)), ]
sensitivity$E <- normalizeBetweenArrays(sensitivity$E, method = "cyclicloess")

shared <- intersect(rownames(proteins), rownames(sensitivity))
tibble(
  slope = c(0.7, round(dpcest$dpc[2], 3)),
  role = c("primary", "sensitivity"),
  n_proteins = c(nrow(proteins), nrow(sensitivity)),
  n_shared = length(shared),
  mean_standard_error = round(c(
    mean(proteins$other$standard.error[shared, ]),
    mean(sensitivity$other$standard.error[shared, ])
  ), 3)
)

round(median(abs(proteins$E[shared, ] - sensitivity$E[shared, ])), 4)

This section renders only when c_data/dpcQuant/proteins_slope_fitted.rds is present, since computing it costs about another 100 minutes. To produce it once:

Rscript 01_Preprocess/02_Quantification/a_script/dpc_quant.R --sensitivity

Afterwards it loads like the primary run does.

Refitting the contrasts under each slope is a separate exercise and is not done here; the counts it produced are recorded in this stage’s README.
